      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go",
      "line": 87,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Failed device tagging is cached, allowing device-limit bypass",
      "body": "tagDeviceUI stores the device ID in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not remove it when CreateOrUpdateDevice fails. If the database returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the first request is rejected, but the cache entry remains for about 29 minutes. A retry with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds, and the device is allowed despite never being admitted under the limit. This makes the configurable limit ineffective after one failed retry per device ID and also masks transient DB errors."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go",
      "line": 110,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "concurrency",
      "title": "Device limit is checked non-atomically before insert",
      "body": "CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active anonymous devices and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate statement without a transaction, row lock, or conditional insert. Under concurrent requests from new device IDs, multiple callers can observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, causing the stored active device count to exceed the configured limit."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go",
      "line": 44,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "perf",
      "title": "Device tagging DB queries are now synchronous in anonymous authentication",
      "body": "Anonymous.Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously. When device_limit is enabled and a device is not in the local cache, this executes a COUNT over anon_device plus an insert/update before authentication completes. Unique device IDs can force this path on every request, adding latency to anonymous logins and creating a DB load vector that did not exist when tagging ran asynchronously with a timeout."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go",
      "line": 120,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "security",
      "title": "Missing X-Grafana-Device-Id bypasses the device limit",
      "body": "TagDevice returns nil immediately when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is absent, and Anonymous.Authenticate then returns an anonymous identity. Because the limit is only enforced for requests that supply this client-controlled header, a client can avoid being counted or blocked simply by omitting the header. If the limit is intended to cap anonymous access, this is a bypass."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go",
      "line": 113,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "untagDevice logs the wrong error variable",
      "body": "When anonStore.DeleteDevice fails, untagDevice logs the outer err variable, which has already been checked to be nil, instead of errD returned by DeleteDevice. The resulting log message does not contain the actual deletion error."

      "title": "Negative device_limit is silently treated as unlimited",
      "body": "AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0), and anonstore only enforces the limit when deviceLimit > 0. A negative configuration value therefore disables limiting instead of being rejected or clamped to zero, which can hide operator mistakes."

There is no test that a limit-reached failure is returned consistently on retries, that the local cache does not mask a failed create, or that existing active devices can still update when the limit is reached."

findings.title: Failed device tagging is cached, allowing device-limit bypass
findings.body: tagDeviceUI stores the device ID in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not remove it when CreateOrUpdateDevice fails. If the database returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the first request is rejected, but the cache entry remains for about 29 minutes. A retry with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds, and the device is allowed despite never being admitted under the limit. This makes the configurable limit ineffective after one failed retry per device ID and also masks transient DB errors.

findings.title: Device limit is checked non-atomically before insert
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active anonymous devices and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate statement without a transaction, row lock, or conditional insert. Under concurrent requests from new device IDs, multiple callers can observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, causing the stored active device count to exceed the configured limit.

findings.title: Device tagging DB queries are now synchronous in anonymous authentication
findings.body: Anonymous.Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously. When device_limit is enabled and a device is not in the local cache, this executes a COUNT over anon_device plus an insert/update before authentication completes. Unique device IDs can force this path on every request, adding latency to anonymous logins and creating a DB load vector that did not exist when tagging ran asynchronously with a timeout.

findings.title: Missing X-Grafana-Device-Id bypasses the device limit
findings.body: TagDevice returns nil immediately when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is absent, and Anonymous.Authenticate then returns an anonymous identity. Because the limit is only enforced for requests that supply this client-controlled header, a client can avoid being counted or blocked simply by omitting the header. If the limit is intended to cap anonymous access, this is a bypass.

findings.title: untagDevice logs the wrong error variable
findings.body: When anonStore.DeleteDevice fails, untagDevice logs the outer err variable, which has already been checked to be nil, instead of errD returned by DeleteDevice. The resulting log message does not contain the actual deletion error.

findings.title: Negative device_limit is silently treated as unlimited
findings.body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0), and anonstore only enforces the limit when deviceLimit > 0. A negative configuration value therefore disables limiting instead of being rejected or clamped to zero, which can hide operator mistakes.

findings.title: No tests cover device-limit enforcement and cache interaction
findings.body: The updated tests use setting.NewCfg(), whose AnonymousDeviceLimit defaults to 0, and assert TagDevice never errors. There is no test that a limit-reached failure is returned consistently on retries, that the local cache does not mask a failed create, or that existing active devices can still update when the limit is reached.
